questions.question: Question 1
questions.solution_html:
• Lack of Substitutes: Necessities often have few or no close substitutes (e.g., basic food items
  • medicines), so people continue to buy them even if prices increase.
  • Marginal Cost (MC) = Marginal Revenue (MR)
  • In perfect competition, MR = Price (P), since the firm is a price taker.
  • Introduction -(2 mark)
  • Explain briefly: Total Product (TP): Total output produced by all units of input.; Average Product (AP)
  • Output per unit of input (TP ÷ units of input); Marginal Product (MP): Additional output by adding one
  • more unit of input (Change in TP).
  • Introduction to Production Function -(2 mark)
  • A production function shows the relationship between input and output. It tells us how much output
  • can be produced using different combinations of inputs.
  • Definition of Economics -(4 mark)
  • Classical Definition – Adam Smith (Wealth-focused): "Economics is the study of the nature and causes of
  • the wealth of nations."
  • Modern Definition – Lionel Robbins (Scarcity-focused): "Economics is the science which studies human
  • behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means which have alternative uses."
  • Amartya Sen’s View (Welfare and development): Economics is also about improving quality of life
  • reducing poverty, and achieving development.
questions.final_answer: reducing poverty, and achieving development

  • 6b. What is unitary elastic demand? Illustrate with a diagram.
  • Unitary elastic demand refers to a situation where if the price of a good changes by a certain
  • percentage, then the quantity demanded or supplied for those good changes by that same
  • percentage. The price elasticity of demand (PED) = 1. -(2 mark)
  • Characteristics
  • A 1% increase in price leads to a 1% decrease in quantity demanded, and vice versa.
  • Total expenditure (or total revenue) remains unchanged when price changes. –(0.5 mark)
  • Example
  • If the price of a good increases from ₹100 to ₹110 (a 10% rise), and the quantity demanded decreases
  • from 50 units to 45 units (a 10% fall), the demand is unitary elastic. –(0.5 mark)
  • Diagram-(2 mark)for diagram
  • 7a. Describe how a perfectly competitive firm maximizes its profits, based on analysis of total revenue
  • total cost curves, and marginal cost curves.
  • Using Total Revenue and Total Cost -(2 mark)
  • A firm earns the most profit when the gap between total revenue (TR) and total cost (TC) is the
  • biggest.
  • TR is a straight line going up (because price stays the same), and TC is a curve that first increases
  • slowly, then faster.
  • The biggest vertical distance between TR and TC shows maximum profit.
  • Using Marginal Cost and Marginal Revenue -(2 mark)
  • A firm finds maximum profit where marginal cost (MC) is equal to marginal revenue (MR).
  • Profit Condition -(1 mark)
  • If the price is more than average total cost (ATC), the firm makes extra (supernormal) profit.

  • Primary Sector –(1 mark)
  • activities like farming, fishing, mining, and forestry. provides raw materials and employs a large
  • Secondary Sector -(1 mark)
  • Covers manufacturing and construction. Converts raw materials into finished goods and supports
  • industrial growth.
  • Tertiary Sector -(1 mark)
  • Includes services like banking, transport, education, and healthcare. It is the fastest-growing sector
  • and contributes the most to India’s GDP.
  • Conclusion – Role of Sectors -(1 mark)
  • All three sectors are interlinked and important for balanced growth. Government policies aim to
  • develop all sectors for a strong economy.
  • 8b. The share of the Indian agriculture sector to GDP is declining throughout the last 5 decades. Does
  • this mean the sector is losing its importance? Justify your answer.
  • Introduction – Declining Share in GDP-(1 mark)
  • Yes, the percentage contribution of agriculture to GDP has been declining steadily due to faster
  • growth of the industrial and service sectors.
  • No, It Is Not Losing Importance (Justification) -(3 mark)–(1 mark)each

  • It supports livelihoods directly and indirectly.
  • b. Food Security; It provides food for the nation, making it essential for survival and stability.
  • c. Raw Material Supply: Agriculture supports many industries (like textiles, food processing) by
  • supplying raw materials.
  • Conclusion – Balanced View -(1 mark)
  • • Although its GDP share is shrinking, agriculture remains economically and socially vital.
  • • Focus should be on modernizing and improving productivity in the sector.

  • A choice between two options for each question, answer two Long essay questions, one from each pair

  • Allocation of Resources: Economics studies how to allocate resources efficiently.

questions.question: Question 3
questions.solution_html:
• Small Proportion of Income: Some necessities, like salt or soap, take up a small portion of a
  • consumer’s income. Even large percentage price increases do not significantly affect the budget
  • so buying patterns remain unchanged.
  • Graphical Representation –(6 mark)
  • Draw 3 curves on the same graph
  • TP Curve: Rises, flattens, and then falls.
  • AP and MP Curves: MP rises, reaches a peak, then declines and becomes negative. And AP rises, peaks
  • and then falls, but MP cuts AP at its maximum point.
  • Suitable Example with Calculation -(6 mark)
  • Importance of Economics in Society -(10 mark)–(2 mark)each
  • a. Helps in Optimal Use of Resources; b. Supports Government Policy Making; c. Promotes Economic
  • Growth and Development; d. Helps in planning for industrial, agricultural, and service sector growth; e.
  • Improves Standard of Living, Helps Understand Global Issues
questions.final_answer: Improves Standard of Living, Helps Understand Global Issues

questions.question: Question 4
questions.solution_html:
• Habitual Consumption: People tend to consume necessities out of habit, and habits are not easily
  • broken by price changes.
  • 2a. A farmer hires two additional workers during the harvest season without buying extra land or tools.
  • Is the farmer changing the level of production or the scale of production? Justify.
  • The farmer is changing the level of production, not the scale of production.(1 mark)
  • When any firm increases production by increasing the quantity of one factor input whereas the
  • quantity of other factor inputs keeping constant; it increases the level of production.(1 mark)
  • In this case, the farmer hires two more workers, which is a variable input, while the land and tools
  • (fixed inputs) remain the same.(0.5 mark)
  • This kind of change occurs in the short run, where the scale of production (which involves
  • proportional changes in all inputs) remains unchanged.(0.5 mark)
  • 2b. Why does the average fixed cost always decline as output increases? Give a real- life example.
  • The Average Fixed Cost (AFC) always declines as output increases because fixed costs remain constant
  • regardless of the level of production, while they are spread over a larger number of units as output
  • increases.(2 mark)
  • Fixed costs (e.g., rent, machinery, salaries of permanent staff) do not change with the level of output.
  • AFC = Total Fixed Cost ÷ Quantity of Output
  • As output (denominator) increases, the same fixed cost is divided by a larger number, causing the
  • average fixed cost to fall.
  • Any example -(1 mark)
  • 3a. Mention the condition for equilibrium of a firm under perfect competition.
  • Under perfect competition, a firm reaches equilibrium when it is producing the right amount of goods
  • to make the most profit possible. At this point, the money it earns from selling one more unit (marginal
  • revenue) is equal to the cost of making that extra unit (marginal cost).(2 mark)
  • The two key conditions for equilibrium are:(0.5 mark)each
  • Interpretation of Results -(4 mark)
  • Stage I: TP increases at increasing rate, MP rising. Efficient use of labour.
  • Stage II: TP increases at decreasing rate. MP and AP fall. Best stage for production—rational
  • region of production.
  • Stage III: TP falls, MP becomes negative. Too many workers reduce efficiency.
  • Characteristics of Cobb-Douglas Function -(2 mark)
  • Shows returns to scale depending on the values of a and b
  • Conclusion -(2 mark)
  • Economics is more than just money or markets—it is about human well-being, decision-making, and the
  • functioning of the society. It helps individuals, businesses, and governments make informed, rational
  • choices in daily life.
  • 10b. "A consumer is willing to buy 5 kg of apples at ₹50 per kg but only 3 kg when the price rises to ₹70
  • per kg." (i) Define demand and explain the relationship between price and quantity demanded in this
  • scenario. (ii) How does this situation reflect the Law of Demand? Support your answer with a demand
  • schedule and diagram. (iii) Give two real-world examples where demand does not strictly follow the Law
  • of Demand.
  • (i) Definition of Demand & Price-Quantity Relationship with suitable example -(8 mark)
  • (ii) Law of Demand with Schedule & Diagram-(8 mark)
  • (iii) Exceptions to the Law of Demand with two real world example -(4 mark)
